candidates.attacker_control: The entire `Authorization: Digest ...` request header is attacker-controlled: username, realm, nonce, uri, response, qop, nc and cnonce. DigestData parses these values (lines 335-356) and validateAndDecode (lines 358-439) only enforces presence/syntax/realm, not the nonce signature. The attacker also controls the declared nonce expiry (first token), which is parsed at line 420 and later trusted by isNonceExpired() (line 451-454).
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that the flaw does not remove the password requirement: the digest response must still match MD5 computed from the stored password/HA1 (lines 169-210), so this is not a passwordless login bypass by itself. Verified the surrounding checks (realm equality line 385, Base64 encoding 392-401, two-token format 407-415, numeric expiry 419-427) and that all other exception constructions in this class and in main code use `throw`; this bare instantiation is unique (searched `new BadCredentialsException` across **/src/main/java/**). Verified the existing invalid-signature test uses an already-expired nonce ("123456"), so it returns 401 via the expiry path (lines 451-454) and does not exercise the missing throw; a non-expired forged nonce was not executed, per review constraints. Considered that DigestAuthenticationFilter is opt-in and that replay also benefits from the absent request-URI binding (calculateServerDigest uses the header `uri`, not request.getRequestURI()) — noted separately rather than merged.
candidates.impact: The server's nonce integrity and lifetime guarantees are bypassed: a client-forged nonce (arbitrary future expiry, arbitrary/absent signature) is accepted. In a capture/MITM scenario this defeats the nonce-expiry limitation and turns a short-lived captured Digest `Authorization` header into an indefinitely replayable credential for that realm (replay/impersonation, access to protected resources as the victim), and it defeats the intended 300s stale-nonce renegotiation policy (DigestAuthenticationEntryPoint nonceValiditySeconds default). The `DigestAuthenticationFilter.nonceCompromised` rejection path is unreachable, contrary to the message catalog (core/.../messages.properties line 25) and the existing test's stated intent (`testNonceWithIncorrectSignatureForNumericFieldReturnsForbidden`, lines 240-256).
candidates.prerequisites: The application must have DigestAuthenticationFilter enabled with a DigestAuthenticationEntryPoint (opt-in; not part of default HttpSecurity/Basic auth). The attacker must supply a `response` digest that the server recomputes successfully, which requires either (a) knowledge of the user's password (malicious client), or (b) capture/MITM of a valid digest exchange in which the attacker influences the nonce (e.g., intercepting the 401 challenge), so the victim computes the response for an attacker-chosen future-dated, unsigned nonce. No server-side privileges are required.
candidates.root_cause: In DigestAuthenticationFilter.DigestData.validateAndDecode, the expected nonce signature is computed as md5Hex(nonceExpiryTime + ":" + entryPointKey) and compared with the client-supplied nonce's second token. When they differ, a BadCredentialsException (message key DigestAuthenticationFilter.nonceCompromised) is instantiated at line 434 but never thrown (no `throw` keyword), so control falls through and validation succeeds. Only nonce syntax (Base64, two ':'-separated tokens, numeric expiry) is enforced; the nonce is therefore not bound to the server key or to a server-issued expiry. DigestAuthenticationEntryPoint (lines 89-101) issues nonces as base64(expiry + ":" + md5Hex(expiry + ":" + key)) precisely so the server can detect forged/tampered nonces; that protection is a no-op here. The later isNonceExpired() check (line 216) trusts the attacker-supplied expiry value, so a future-dated forged nonce passes.
candidates.title: Digest Authentication nonce-integrity check is created but never thrown, so unverified/forged nonces are accepted
candidates.trace: 1) Request with `Authorization: Digest ... nonce=...` reaches DigestAuthenticationFilter.doFilter (line 123-146). 2) DigestData is constructed from the header and validateAndDecode(key, realm) is invoked inside a try/catch that would fail the request on BadCredentialsException (lines 136-146). 3) validateAndDecode passes realm/format checks and reaches the signature comparison at line 433; on mismatch it calls `new BadCredentialsException(...)` (line 434) but does not throw, so no exception reaches the catch block. 4) The server digest is recomputed with the password, the actual HTTP method and the attacker-supplied `uri`/nonce/nc/cnonce (lines 169-184, 441-449) and compared to the supplied `response` (line 198). 5) The only remaining nonce check, isNonceExpired() (line 216), compares the attacker-supplied expiry token to the current time; a forged nonce with a far-future expiry passes. 6) An authenticated UsernamePasswordAuthenticationToken (or empty-context variant) is placed into the SecurityContext and the chain proceeds (lines 230-235).
candidates.unverified: No code was executed and no runtime confirmation exists; the practical replay scenario requires the attacker to obtain a valid digest response for an attacker-influenced nonce (MITM/capture) or to be a client knowing the password, so real-world exploitability is argued from source semantics only. I could not verify the upstream fixing commit or advisory mapping from within this snapshot. The related gap that DigestData.uri is not compared to the actual request URI (so a captured header can be replayed to a different path within the nonce window) exists but is a distinct defect and is left as an unconfirmed lead. Security-critical areas reviewed only by sampling include reactive web/oauth2 flows, config module wiring, and most of the acl/ldap/cas/openid modules.
candidates.weakness_type: Improper Authentication — nonce integrity/expiry validation bypass (CWE-287/CWE-294-like, replay protection defeat)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 2,855 files under the repository root, 2,854 visible to the model (1 excluded for a sensitive name; 0 binary-like files >5 MiB, binary detection only skips files with NUL bytes in the first 8 KiB). The P1 relation index covers 2,854 files with 2,308 parsed Java files, 23,500 symbols, 78,768 call sites and 46,661 edges; 409 files were omitted and the index reports no control-flow/data-flow/semantic resolution and an overall 'partial' status, so index absence does not imply review of an area. Selection (as the rubric allows) is not exhaustive; I did not read every file. Modules reached by direct reading include web (filters, firewalls, request matchers/saved requests, remember-me, CSRF, headers, async context, Digest/Basic authentication, server/reactive pieces sampled), core (voters, access-decision managers, provider manager/DAO provider, userdetails/JDBC/LDAP integrations sampled), oauth2 client/core/jose/resource-server (authorization request/response handling, OIDC token validation, JWT decoders, bearer resolution), config (HttpSecurity configurers and MvcRequestMatcher), acl, crypto/password, ldap, cas, openid, messaging, taglibs and test-support modules sampled. Custom file/URL handling, SQL construction, XML parsing and deserialization sinks were searched globally; no obvious injection/deserialization sink was found in main code.
limitations: Read-only review; no code was executed, no tests were run, and no runtime/exploit confirmation was performed.

The P1 relation index provides syntactic navigation candidates only: no data-flow, control-flow, semantic resolution, Spring DI/runtime reachability or security enforcement proof; 409 files were omitted from indexing.
The benchmark/ground-truth vulnerability mapping (e.g., which upstream fixing commit or CVE this snapshot corresponds to) was not verified from inside the snapshot and is deliberately not asserted.

Coverage was broad but not byte-by-byte: deeper review focused on authentication/authorization, request-path handling and OAuth2/OIDC; the reactive web/oauth2 stacks, config XML/annotation wiring, acl internals, ldap/cas/openid details and sample apps were only sampled.

The Digest finding's exploitability depends on the deployment enabling DigestAuthenticationFilter and on the attacker's ability to influence/capture a digest exchange with a valid response (or knowledge of the password); the replay-across-URI gap in the same class was noted but not fully validated.
Binary-like and sensitive-name files were skipped by the tooling (1 file excluded, 0 over the size cap), so no claim is made about those files.

rejected_leads.lead: OIDC ID Token validation gaps in OidcTokenValidator (issuer validation TODO gh-4413, nonce TODO gh-4442, alg TODO gh-4413); createOidcToken uses NimbusJwtDecoderJwkSupport with the default timestamp-only validator in OidcAuthorizationCodeAuthenticationProvider.
rejected_leads.reason: The gaps are explicitly documented upstream TODOs in this snapshot and the decoder still verifies signatures against the client registration's configured JWKS; no attacker-controlled issuer key path was found, so impact and regression evidence are weaker than the Digest candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: StrictHttpFirewall accepts control/NUL characters in percent-encoded form because containsOnlyPrintableAsciiCharacters checks only the raw request URI and the blacklists contain no NUL/control entries.
rejected_leads.reason: No concrete bypass could be demonstrated: Java servlet containers generally reject %00/control characters before the filter chain, and no code path was found where a decoded NUL/control character changes a security decision. Remains an unconfirmed hardening gap.

rejected_leads.lead: OAuth2AuthorizationCodeGrantFilter / DefaultSavedRequest redirect handling and OAuth2 login request resolution (potential open-redirect/replay surfaces).
rejected_leads.reason: Traced the state-bound session lookups and redirect-URL construction; comparisons are bound to session-stored values and no attacker-controlled redirect target was identified in the snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: OnCommittedResponseWrapper does not override setHeader/setContentLengthLong for Content-Length tracking, so HeaderWriterFilter/SecurityContext saving may not run before commit when apps set Content-Length via setHeader.
rejected_leads.reason: Impact would be missing security headers or late SecurityContext persistence rather than an authentication bypass, and no attacker-controlled trigger was established; not explored further.

rejected_leads.lead: DefaultLoginPageGeneratingFilter / DefaultLogoutPageGeneratingFilter render hidden input name/value pairs without HTML escaping, and CsrfMetaTagsTag/CsrfInputTag interpolate token values unescaped.
rejected_leads.reason: The values originate from the CSRF token and server-side client-registration names (client names are escaped at line 283), not from attacker-controlled request data, so exploitability was not established.

summary: Reviewed the assigned Spring Security snapshot (version 5.2.0.BUILD-SNAPSHOT; ~2.3k Java files across core/web/config/acl/crypto/ldap/cas/openid/messaging/oauth2/taglibs/test). Broad tracing of attacker-influenced input through request matchers/firewalls, OAuth2/OIDC clients, remember-me, CSRF, session and ACL code did not yield a stronger concrete defect than one in the HTTP Digest authentication filter: the nonce-integrity check in DigestAuthenticationFilter.DigestData.validateAndDecode computes the expected nonce signature and, on mismatch, creates a BadCredentialsException without throwing it. This is the only bare (non-thrown) exception construction found in main code, it makes the "Nonce token compromised" rejection dead code, and it means the nonce is never bound to the server key/expiry value. The single candidate below is submitted as a lead with source evidence only; exploit conditions include the filter being enabled and the attacker having/capturing a valid digest response for a nonce they can influence (e.g., MITM/capture scenario or a client that knows the password).
